title: Longest Happy Prefix
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing every candidate length directly versus the KMP prefix-suffix array.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, a "happy prefix" is a non empty proper prefix that is also a proper suffix of the same string (proper meaning it cannot be the entire string itself). Return the longest such happy prefix, or an empty string if none exists.

blocks.text: Given a string s, a "happy prefix" is a non empty proper prefix that is also a proper suffix of the same string (proper meaning it cannot be the entire string itself). Return the longest such happy prefix, or an empty string if none exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Word That Starts and Ends the Same Way
blocks.text: Like noticing that a long word both starts and ends with the exact same shorter chunk of letters, the way "level" both starts and ends with the letter "l".

blocks.caption: Find the longest chunk that is both a genuine prefix and a genuine suffix of the string

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Prefixes: l, le, lev, leve. Suffixes: l, el, vel, evel","only \"l\" appears in both lists","no longer prefix matches its same length suffix"],["Answer","\"l\"","the single character l is the longest common prefix and suffix"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The prefix \"abab\" and the suffix \"abab\" (the last 4 characters) match exactly","the longest such match","the repeating ab pattern lets a 4 character chunk align at both ends"],["Answer","\"abab\"","no longer prefix and suffix pair (of length 5) can match, since that would require matching the entire string against itself shifted by one"]]}

blocks.text: The prefix "leet" and the last 4 characters "leet" match exactly, and no longer prefix and suffix pair matches, giving "leet".
It helps to ask whether this problem is really asking for something new, or for something already computed as a side effect of a technique seen before.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force tries every candidate length from longest to shortest, directly comparing a prefix against a same length suffix, recomputing the comparison completely from scratch at every single length.

Observation 2: Repeated Substring Pattern already introduced building the "longest proper prefix that is also a suffix" array, the KMP preprocessing step, in a single linear pass, capturing exactly this self overlap information for every position at once.

Observation 3: The value stored at the very last position of that array is, by its own definition, exactly the length of the longest proper prefix of the whole string that is also a proper suffix of the whole string, which is precisely what a happy prefix is.

Observation 4: This means no separate search is needed at all once the array is built, the answer is simply read directly off its last entry, confirmed by tracing s equal to "ababab" through the array (0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4) to the correct answer, "abab", using the exact same construction already seen in Repeated Substring Pattern.
Recognizing that a happy prefix is exactly the value the KMP prefix-suffix array already stores at its last position is what turns this problem into a direct lookup instead of a fresh search.
Starting from the longest possible proper prefix length and working downward, directly compare each candidate prefix against the same length suffix, and return the first length that produces a match.

items: For every candidate length from n minus 1 down to 1, extract the prefix and the suffix of that length.
Compare them directly for equality.
Return the first (and therefore longest) length that matches.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Candidate lengths are tried from longest to shortest, so the very first match found is guaranteed to be the longest possible one.
The upper bound n minus 1 enforces that the match must be a proper prefix and suffix, never the entire string itself.
Each candidate length triggers a fresh, independent substring comparison, with no information carried over from previously tried lengths.

blocks.text: Trying every candidate length from longest to shortest and directly comparing correctly finds the longest happy prefix, if one exists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), comparing up to n characters for each of up to n candidate lengths.
Space: O(n), for the substrings being compared.

Limitation: each candidate length is checked completely independently, recomputing the comparison from scratch, when the same underlying structural information (how much of the string matches itself at different offsets) can be computed once, incrementally.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: comparing each candidate prefix and suffix pair independently throws away the fact that shorter matches are closely related to longer ones through the string's own internal structure.

What the prefix-suffix array fixes directly: building it once captures, at every position, how much of the prefix ending there overlaps with a suffix ending there, in a single linear pass.

Why the last position specifically answers this problem: by definition, the array's value at the final index is exactly the longest proper prefix of the entire string that is also a proper suffix of the entire string.

The core idea: build the array once, then read the answer directly from its last entry, with no further comparison needed.

Build the KMP "longest proper prefix which is also a suffix" array for the string in a single linear pass. This is exactly the same preprocessing step used by the KMP string matching algorithm. The value of this array at the very last position directly gives the length of the longest happy prefix, with no further searching needed.
Build the prefix-suffix array once, and read the answer directly from its last value.

blocks.caption: Optimized: the prefix-suffix array's final value directly gives the answer's length

blocks.text: This works because the prefix-suffix array is built precisely to track, at every position, the length of the longest prefix of the string that matches a suffix ending at that position, so at the very final position, which spans the entire string, that tracked value is by construction exactly the longest proper prefix that is also a proper suffix of the whole string.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), building the prefix-suffix array in a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the prefix-suffix array.

blocks.text: This problem is essentially asking directly for the value that the KMP preprocessing step computes anyway, making it an excellent way to build genuine intuition for what the prefix-suffix array actually represents before applying it to full pattern matching problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "have you seen this array before", think: yes, it is exactly the KMP prefix-suffix array from Repeated Substring Pattern, just read differently.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid comparing every candidate length", think: build the prefix-suffix array once and read the answer from its last value.
If the interviewer says "what does the prefix-suffix array actually represent", think: at every position, the length of the longest prefix of the string that also matches a suffix ending there.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space. Optimized (KMP prefix-suffix array): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: the Knuth-Morris-Pratt prefix-suffix (LPS) array, whose final value directly answers the question.
Core Idea: the longest happy prefix is, by definition, exactly the value the KMP prefix-suffix array already stores at its very last position, so building that array once is the entire solution.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: a problem can sometimes be exactly a known algorithm's preprocessing step, read directly, rather than a new problem requiring new machinery.
Interview Difficulty: trivial once the KMP array is recognized as directly relevant; genuinely hard if approached as a brand new problem without that recognition.
One line memory trick: build the KMP prefix-suffix array, the answer is sitting right there in its last entry.
